CVE-2026-116474.title: Gitea Actions job token spoofing of instance-signed commits
CVE-2026-116474.description: The `GITEA_TOKEN` of a Gitea Actions job authenticates as the `gitea-actions` system user, and the `/api/v1/user` email and GPG key endpoints accepted that user, so a job could register an email address and a GPG key on it; without required email confirmation (the default) the address is stored as activated. Commit verification treats a key without a real owner as the instance signing key, so any user who can run a workflow job could make commits signed with their own key show as trusted and signed by the instance in every repository where they appear, including pull requests to repositories the user cannot write to. The impact is limited to the displayed signature status: enforcement such as required signed commits only checks that a signature is verified and is unaffected, and no access is gained. The `/api/v1/user` routes now reject system users.

CVE-2026-133620.title: Flowintel Template Repository Path Traversal and Symlink Escape Allows Arbitrary File Read
CVE-2026-133620.description:
Flowintel's template repository subsystem did not adequately constrain file access to the configured repository base directory. Two related weaknesses existed:

- Repository registration and editing accepted arbitrary local paths without verifying they resolved inside the configured REPOSITORY_BASE_PATH, allowing an authenticated user to point a repository at any readable directory on the host.

Affected: Flowintel versions prior to 4.1.0.

CVE-2026-98958.title: wifi: mt76: account non-AQL frames per peer rather than per link
CVE-2026-98958.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: mt76: account non-AQL frames per peer rather than per link

hardware queue. The completion path decrements the counter again.

For an MLO peer, the hardware reports the completion on the link that it
used for the transmission. This link can differ from the link that the
driver queued the frame on. In that case, the increment and the
decrement go to different link wcids, and the count drifts upwards until
it blocks the station.

Keep the count on the wcid of the primary link, like the other peer-wide
state.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: dc395x: sync the waiting_timer before freeing the host

The waiting_timer callback re-arms itself and takes the host lock.
adapter_uninit() currently stops it with timer_delete(), which does not
wait for a callback already running on another CPU. The final
scsi_host_put() that frees the host (and the host lock the callback
dereferences) runs right after adapter_uninit(), so a concurrent or just
re-armed callback can fire after the free, leaving a potential
use-after-free window.

Replace timer_delete() with timer_shutdown_sync() at the top of
adapter_uninit(), before the host-lock section: the timer is dequeued,
a running callback is waited for and rearming is blocked before the chip
is halted, so it cannot fire at all once the adapter has ceased to
function. Waiting outside the lock avoids the self-deadlock that would
result from syncing a callback blocked on the lock we still hold.

CVE-2026-99522.title: RDMA/irdma: avoid use-after-free in icrdma_remove
CVE-2026-99522.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

RDMA/irdma: avoid use-after-free in icrdma_remove

icrdma_remove() dereferences iwdev after calling
irdma_ib_unregister_device():

irdma_ib_unregister_device(iwdev)
-> ib_unregister_device(&iwdev->ibdev)
-> __ib_unregister_device()
-> ib_dealloc_device()

irdma registers irdma_ib_dealloc_device() as the dealloc_driver
callback in its ib_device_ops. The RDMA core explicitly documents
ib_unregister_device() that when ops.dealloc_driver is used, ib_dev
will be freed upon return from the function.

The ib_device is embedded in struct irdma_device and iwdev itself was
allocated by ib_alloc_device(irdma_device, ibdev). Consequently, once
irdma_ib_unregister_device() returns, iwdev must no longer be
dereferenced.

However, icrdma_remove() currently accesses iwdev->rf afterwards when
deinitializing interrupts, destroying ah_tbl_lock, and freeing rf.

CVE-2026-99597.title: srcu: Add list_splice_init_srcu()
CVE-2026-99597.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

srcu: Add list_splice_init_srcu()

list_splice_init_rcu() makes a list look empty to new readers, waits for
the current ones with the given sync function, and only then links the
entries into the new list. The sync function takes no argument, so it
can wait for RCU readers but not for the readers of an srcu_struct.

Passing synchronize_rcu() for a list read under SRCU still builds, but
leaves SRCU readers on the entries while the last one's next pointer is
moved onto the new list head. nvme_remove_namespaces() does this today.

Add list_splice_init_srcu(), which waits for the readers of the given
srcu_struct instead.

CVE-2026-99711.title: KVM: nVMX: Process each host MSR entry at most once when unwinding failed VM-Entry
CVE-2026-99711.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: nVMX: Process each host MSR entry at most once when unwinding failed VM-Entry

Add a missing "break" in the inner for-loop of the open coded mess that
unwinds MSRs back to the pre-VM-Enter state when VMLAUNCH/VMRESUME VM-Fails
due to a consistency check that is caught by hardware but missed by KVM.
I.e. move on to the next MSR in the VM-Entry load list after performing a
write using a value found in the VM-Exit load list. Processing *every*
matching entry in the VM-Exit load list makes the processing quadratic,
which is problematic if the load lists are full of MSRs that are expensive
to emulate. E.g. writing APIC_BASE triggers kvm_recalculate_apic_map() and
a whole pile of unnecessary work.

Functionally, arbitrarily restoring the value of the first matching entry
is "fine", because none of this is architecturally correct: the load lists
are never supposed to have been used in the first place. In practice,…
